name: Personalised Learning and Early Warning
title: Personalised Learning and Early Warning
answer: Personalised learning and early warning sit within course design and teaching as two connected practices. Personalised learning adjusts pace, sequence, examples, and feedback to a learner's current knowledge and goals. Early warning uses data from a course to flag students who may need support before a final failure or withdrawal. Together they ask how instruction can respond to individual progress while keeping the whole cohort visible. The topic covers both the design of adaptive activities and the design of alert rules, dashboards, and interventions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Personalised learning and early warning sit within course design and teaching as two connected practices. Personalised learning adjusts pace, sequence, examples, and feedback to a learner's current knowledge and goals. Early warning uses data from a course to flag students who may need support before a final failure or withdrawal. Together they ask how instruction can respond to individual progress while keeping the whole cohort visible. The topic covers both the design of adaptive activities and the design of alert rules, dashboards, and interventions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on the ordinary infrastructure of a course: a learning management system, a student information system, an assessment platform, and a gradebook. They draw on data such as logins, page views, quiz attempts, assignment submissions, discussion posts, attendance, and prior grades. A dashboard or alert service may sit on top, sending messages to instructors or advisers. The infrastructure must handle identity, permissions, data refresh, and the plain fact that a course changes week by week. Some deployments use a data warehouse or a learning record store, while others start with a spreadsheet and a weekly report.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: On the personalised side, teams map learning objectives to content and then define rules or models that choose the next activity, hint, or practice item. On the early warning side, they define a risk outcome, such as a low midterm score or non submission, and then build a simple model or threshold rule from historical course data. Common methods include logistic regression, decision trees, and simple counts of missed deadlines, chosen for interpretability as much as accuracy. The site's library of 135 research papers and 12646 claims can support a review of what has been tried, and the site links to original papers rather than a search tool. Evaluation uses held out terms or past cohorts, with attention to false alarms and missed students.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Student data is sensitive, so provenance matters: where each field comes from, who can see it, how long it is kept, and what it is used for. Early warning labels can stigmatise, and a flag is not a diagnosis or a prediction of a person's future. Personalisation can narrow a learner's exposure if it only offers what an algorithm thinks they can handle. Institutions need clear rules for consent, access, retention, and appeal, plus a way for students to see and correct their data. Any model or rule should be documented with its training data, its known limits, and the intervention it is meant to trigger.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving from static dashboards toward timely, context aware support that reaches students inside the tools they already use. Personalisation is shifting from fixed learning paths to adaptive practice and feedback that can be explained to a learner. Early warning is moving from a single risk score to a set of signals that instructors can inspect and act on with human judgement. Larger language models may help draft feedback or summarise progress, but they also raise new questions about accuracy, bias, and privacy. The durable direction is less about prediction alone and more about closing the loop between a signal, a conversation, and a change in teaching.
